description: Country-specific GeoGuessr visual meta identifiers. tier1 = highly distinctive and reliable. tier2 = supporting evidence. elimination_clues = how to distinguish from common confusions.

tier1_identifiers: White utility poles with multiple horizontal crossbars in specific Japanese style
Hiragana, Katakana, or Kanji script on all signs
Specific Japanese road sign shape and color (blue with white text, rounded corners)
Vending machines visible on roadsides
Specific Japanese road mirror (convex circular mirror) at intersections
Rice paddies in rural areas
tier2_identifiers: Very clean and well-maintained road surfaces
Specific Japanese guardrail style (white with reflectors)
Overhead power lines in very dense clusters
Specific Japanese street light design

elimination_clues.vs_South_Korea: Korean script (Hangul) looks very different from Japanese. Japanese has far more roadside vending machines. Japanese utility poles have very distinctive crossbar clustering.
elimination_clues.vs_Taiwan: Taiwan has Traditional Chinese characters mixed with Bopomofo phonetic script. Japanese uses a distinct mix of Hiragana, Katakana, and Kanji.

tier1_identifiers: Hangul script on signs (distinctive rounded Korean characters unlike any other script)
Specific Korean road sign style (green with white text for highways)
Korean apartment block style — very tall numbered residential blocks with prominent numbers
Specific Korean utility pole style — concrete poles with distinct transformer boxes
tier2_identifiers: Korean commercial signage aesthetic (dense colorful shop signs)
Specific Korean street furniture and bus stop design

elimination_clues.vs_Japan: Hangul vs Japanese scripts are clearly different — Hangul uses squares and circles, Japanese uses more complex ideographic characters. South Korea has fewer roadside vending machines than Japan.

tier1_identifiers: Ger (yurt) settlements visible alongside roads
Extremely vast open steppe with virtually no infrastructure for long distances
Specific Mongolian wooden slat fence styles (horizontal wooden boards, often unpainted)
Cyrillic script on signs (Mongolian Cyrillic, different feel from Russian)
Very rough unpaved roads — often just tracks across steppe
Extreme emptiness — no buildings visible for many kilometers
tier2_identifiers: Specific Mongolian utility pole style (often leaning, old Soviet-era)
Traditional Mongolian architectural elements in towns

elimination_clues.vs_Kazakhstan: Mongolia has more extreme emptiness and more ger settlements. Kazakhstan has more Russian-influenced infrastructure and better road quality in many areas.
elimination_clues.vs_Russia: Mongolia has ger settlements not seen in Russia. Russia has better road quality and more modern infrastructure. Mongolian script mixing sometimes visible alongside Cyrillic.

tier1_identifiers: Yellow painted road centerlines (distinctively yellow, not white — very reliable Senegal identifier)
French language on signs
Specific brightly painted Senegalese transport vehicles (sept-place taxis)
Baobab trees visible (large trunk, sparse branches)
Specific West African road infrastructure with French colonial influence
tier2_identifiers: Specific Senegalese painted architecture
West African market infrastructure with French signage

elimination_clues.vs_Nigeria: Senegal is French-speaking with French signs. Nigerian signs are in English. Senegal has yellow road centerlines vs Nigerian white. Nigerian danfo yellow minibuses not present in Senegal.
elimination_clues.vs_Ghana: Ghana is English-speaking. Senegal is French-speaking. This is the most reliable distinguisher.
elimination_clues.vs_Cameroon: Cameroon is bilingual French/English with both on signs. Senegal is French only.

tier1_identifiers: White or cream-colored road bollards (vs Sweden yellow/black — very reliable)
Finnish language on signs (very long compound words, double vowels like 'aa', 'oo', 'ii')
Dense conifer forest pressing right to the road edge
Specific Finnish road sign style (white background, black text, red border)
Lakes visible through trees (Finland has ~180,000 lakes)
tier2_identifiers: Finnish wooden house architecture (often red or yellow painted wood)
Specific Finnish road surface quality and lane markings

elimination_clues.vs_Sweden: Finland has white/cream bollards. Sweden has yellow and black bollards. This is THE most reliable Finland vs Sweden distinguisher. Finnish language has very long compound words unlike Swedish.
elimination_clues.vs_Norway: Norway is dramatically mountainous and fjord-heavy. Finland is much flatter with dense forests and lakes. Norwegian on signs looks like Swedish, not Finnish.
elimination_clues.vs_Estonia: Estonia has shorter, more compact words on signs. Estonian road infrastructure is slightly less maintained than Finnish.

tier1_identifiers: Yellow and black road bollards — highly distinctive, almost unique to Sweden
Swedish language on signs (similar to Norwegian but with specific letter combinations)
Specific Swedish road sign style and colors (blue highways, yellow route numbers)
Swedish Falu red (dark red) wooden houses in rural areas
Specific Swedish highway infrastructure (smooth, well-maintained)
tier2_identifiers: Swedish landscape — mix of forests and lakes, more open than Finland
Specific Swedish utility pole infrastructure

elimination_clues.vs_Finland: Yellow and black bollards = Sweden. White/cream bollards = Finland. This is THE most reliable distinguisher between these two countries.
elimination_clues.vs_Norway: Norway has more dramatic mountain scenery and fjords. Sweden is flatter. Swedish route numbers use yellow on blue, Norwegian use different color scheme.

tier1_identifiers: Yellow centerlines on roads (vs Australian white centerlines — very reliable NZ identifier)
SH prefix on route signs (State Highway — e.g. SH1, SH2)
Specific New Zealand road sign font and style (slightly different from Australian)
Very green rolling hills (greener than most of Australia)
Specific New Zealand farmhouse architecture style
tier2_identifiers: NZ-specific utility pole style
Sheep farming infrastructure and green paddock fencing
Distinctive NZ vegetation mix (introduced and native)

elimination_clues.vs_Australia: NZ has yellow road centerlines, Australia has white. NZ uses SH route prefix, Australia uses different state-based systems. NZ is generally greener and more hilly than most of Australia. NZ has its own specific road sign font.

tier1_identifiers: Yellow danfo minibuses — extremely distinctive Lagos transport, bright yellow
English language on signs
Specific Nigerian road infrastructure — often older, mixed condition
West African market architecture — corrugated iron roofs, dense stalls
Specific Nigerian painted commercial trucks with decorative text
tier2_identifiers: Specific Nigerian utility infrastructure — dense, often chaotic pole wiring
Nigerian commercial signage style — brightly painted shop fronts

elimination_clues.vs_Ghana: Both English-speaking. Nigerian yellow danfo minibuses are very distinctive. Lagos-scale infrastructure. Ghana has different bus styles.
elimination_clues.vs_Cameroon: Cameroon is bilingual French/English with both languages on signs. Nigeria is English only.

tier1_identifiers: Bilingual English and Afrikaans on road signs (e.g. 'STOP / HALT', 'GIVE WAY / GEE PAD')
Specific South African road sign color scheme (green for national routes, blue/white for provincial)
N-prefixed national routes (N1, N2, N3 etc)
Distinctive South African fynbos vegetation (Western Cape — low shrubby heathland)
Cape Dutch whitewashed architecture in Western Cape
tier2_identifiers: South African suburban architecture (walled compounds, security gates)
Specific SA utility pole and power infrastructure

elimination_clues.vs_Botswana: South Africa has much more developed road infrastructure. Afrikaans on signs = South Africa confirmed (not Botswana).
elimination_clues.vs_Namibia: Namibia also has Afrikaans but also German on signs (three languages). South Africa has only English and Afrikaans. SA roads are generally better quality.
elimination_clues.vs_Zimbabwe: Zimbabwe has English only on signs, no Afrikaans. Zimbabwe infrastructure is less maintained.

tier1_identifiers: Distinctive diamond-shaped cattle warning signs on roads — unique to Botswana
Very flat semi-arid landscape with sparse mopane woodland
Sandy soil with sparse bush — specific Kalahari-type terrain
Specific Botswana road sign style (similar to SA but less bilingual)
tier2_identifiers: Specific Botswana infrastructure style — functional but less developed than SA
Okavango-style vegetation in northern Botswana

elimination_clues.vs_South_Africa: Botswana has much less developed road infrastructure than SA. Diamond-shaped cattle warning signs are specific to Botswana. No Afrikaans on Botswana signs.
elimination_clues.vs_Zimbabwe: Zimbabwe more agricultural with more trees. Botswana more arid and flat Kalahari terrain.

tier1_identifiers: Bahasa Indonesia on signs (distinctive long compound words, no tones)
Specific Indonesian road sign style (red and white colors of national flag influence)
Dense tropical vegetation right to road edge
Very high motorcycle traffic density — Indonesia has more motorcycles than almost anywhere
Indonesian Islamic architecture elements — mosques with specific dome styles
tier2_identifiers: Indonesian kampung (village) architecture — zinc roofed small houses clustered densely
Specific road surface quality — often patched asphalt with drainage channels

elimination_clues.vs_Malaysia: Malaysia has trilingual signs (Malay, English, Chinese). Indonesia is almost exclusively Indonesian language. Malaysia roads are generally better quality.
elimination_clues.vs_Philippines: Philippines has heavy English usage on signs. Filipino vehicle styles differ. Philippines more mountainous in Luzon.
elimination_clues.vs_Thailand: Thai script is completely distinctive and unlike any other. If you see Thai script, it is Thailand not Indonesia.

tier1_identifiers: Turkish language on signs — distinctive letters: ş, ğ, ı, ö, ü, ç
Specific Turkish road sign style (green for highways, white for local)
Minarets visible in towns (mosques with tall thin towers)
Specific Turkish utility pole style — often concrete with distinctive brackets
Turkish tea garden (çay bahçesi) infrastructure visible in towns
tier2_identifiers: Specific Turkish architectural style — Ottoman-influenced in older areas
Turkish road surface quality — often good quality highways, varied rural quality

elimination_clues.vs_Greece: Greek script (Α, Β, Γ) vs Turkish Latin script. Greece has more island and coastal feel with specific Greek architecture.
elimination_clues.vs_Bulgaria: Bulgarian uses Cyrillic script. Turkish uses Latin. Very reliable script-based distinguisher.
elimination_clues.vs_Georgia: Georgian script is completely unique and unlike any other alphabet. If you see Georgian script, it is Georgia not Turkey.

tier1_identifiers: Romanian language on signs — distinctive diacritics: ș (s-comma), ț (t-comma), ă (a-breve)
Specific Romanian road sign style (EU-standard green highways, white local)
Romanian Orthodox church architecture — distinctive gold dome style
Specific Eastern European rural house style — plaster walls, often brightly painted gates
Older road infrastructure with specific Eastern European character
tier2_identifiers: Romanian utility pole style — often wooden, Soviet-era influenced in rural areas
Specific Romanian landscape — mix of plains, hills, and Carpathian mountains

elimination_clues.vs_Bulgaria: Bulgarian uses Cyrillic script. Romanian uses Latin script with diacritics. This script difference is completely reliable.
elimination_clues.vs_Hungary: Hungarian has distinctive double-acute accents (ő, ű). Romanian has comma-below diacritics (ș, ț). Different alphabet feel.
elimination_clues.vs_Moldova: Moldova and Romania look very similar. Moldova may have Russian/Cyrillic signs alongside Romanian. Similar architecture.

tier1_identifiers: English language on signs
Specific Kenyan road sign style (similar to British standards, left-hand drive country)
East African savanna vegetation — acacia trees, red laterite soil
Specific Kenyan matatu minibus style — brightly decorated minibuses
Red laterite soil roads are very common in rural Kenya
tier2_identifiers: Specific Kenyan infrastructure — mix of modern and older
East African vernacular architectural style

elimination_clues.vs_Tanzania: Both East African with English. Kenya has more developed infrastructure near Nairobi. Very similar landscapes make these hard to distinguish without city names.
elimination_clues.vs_Ethiopia: Ethiopia uses Amharic script (Ge'ez/Ethiopic script) — completely distinctive. If you see Amharic script, it is Ethiopia, not Kenya.
elimination_clues.vs_Uganda: Very similar. Uganda drives on the left like Kenya. Look for specific road sign differences and city names.

tier1_identifiers: Portuguese language on signs (similar to Spanish but distinct — look for 'ã', 'ç', 'ão' endings)
Specific Brazilian state highway signs (e.g. BA-xxx for Bahia, SP-xxx for Sao Paulo)
Specific Brazilian road sign color scheme (white and blue for state routes)
Diverse terrain from Amazon jungle to Cerrado savanna to Caatinga desert
Specific Brazilian utility pole style in rural areas
tier2_identifiers: Brazilian favela architecture in urban outskirts
Specific Brazilian commercial truck painting style
BR-xxx federal highway signs

elimination_clues.vs_Colombia: Colombian signs use Spanish without the Portuguese 'ão' and 'ã' patterns. Brazilian signs have state prefixes (BA, SP, MG etc). Colombia has distinctive red BRT buses in Bogota.
elimination_clues.vs_Peru: Peru uses Spanish. Very different road infrastructure. Peruvian Andes terrain very distinctive.
elimination_clues.vs_Bolivia: Bolivia uses Spanish. More mountainous terrain. Less developed road infrastructure than coastal Brazil.

tier1_identifiers: White road centerlines (vs New Zealand yellow — very reliable)
Specific Australian road sign font and style (distinctive font, state-specific colors)
Australian state route prefixes (NSW, VIC, QLD, WA, SA, TAS number systems)
Kangaroo or wombat warning signs
Eucalyptus (gum tree) vegetation — very distinctive bark patterns
Specific Australian outback red dirt roads
tier2_identifiers: Australian utility pole style
Specific Australian rural mailbox style
Australian highway infrastructure (STOP signs, give way triangles)

elimination_clues.vs_New_Zealand: Australia has white road centerlines, NZ has yellow. Australian route signs use state abbreviations, NZ uses SH prefix. Australia generally drier and flatter than NZ.
elimination_clues.vs_South_Africa: South Africa has bilingual English/Afrikaans signs. Australia is English only. Very different vegetation types.

tier1_identifiers: Script on signs varies by region — Hindi (Devanagari), Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Bengali etc
NH (National Highway) prefix on route signs
Specific Indian road sign style — yellow background for caution signs
Extremely dense and colorful commercial signage
Specific Indian auto-rickshaw (tuk-tuk) — three-wheeled yellow-black in many states
Colorfully decorated trucks with 'HORN PLEASE' or similar text
tier2_identifiers: Indian utility pole style — dense wiring clusters
Specific Indian road surface quality — often patched with concrete repairs

elimination_clues.vs_Pakistan: Pakistan uses Urdu script (Nastaliq style) on signs. Indian signs use Devanagari or regional scripts. Indian auto-rickshaws often yellow-black, Pakistani ones different.
elimination_clues.vs_Bangladesh: Bangladesh uses Bengali script similar to West Bengal, India. Very hard to distinguish without city names.
elimination_clues.vs_Nepal: Nepali uses Devanagari like Hindi but landscape is much more mountainous. Nepal has very distinctive Himalayan backdrop.

tier1_identifiers: Cyrillic script on all signs (Russian Cyrillic)
Specific Russian federal highway sign style (M-prefix routes)
Soviet-era apartment blocks (khrushchyovka) — 5-story grey concrete blocks
Specific Russian utility pole style — wooden poles, Soviet-era transformers
Russian Orthodox church domes (gold onion domes) visible in towns
tier2_identifiers: Dense birch and pine forests
Russian road surface quality — often poor outside major cities with potholes

elimination_clues.vs_Ukraine: Very similar. Ukraine now often has yellow and blue national colors on infrastructure. Russian signs use standard white/green. Hard to distinguish in rural areas.
elimination_clues.vs_Belarus: Belarus and Russia look very similar. Belarus slightly better road quality in many areas.
elimination_clues.vs_Kazakhstan: Kazakhstan uses both Cyrillic and Latin now. Less dense forests. More steppe landscape.

tier1_identifiers: French language on signs
Specific French road sign style — blue direction signs with white text
Specific French yellow road centerlines in older areas (white more recently)
Plane tree (platane) rows lining rural roads
Specific French town name sign style (white rectangular with black border)
tier2_identifiers: French rural architecture — stone farmhouses, tile roofs
Specific French utility pole style

elimination_clues.vs_Belgium: Belgium has bilingual French and Dutch/Flemish in many areas. French-only signs = more likely France.
elimination_clues.vs_Switzerland: Switzerland has four languages (French, German, Italian, Romansh) and uses CH country code on vehicles. French-speaking Switzerland looks similar to France.

tier1_identifiers: German language on signs (distinctive compound words, ß, ü, ö, ä)
Specific German Autobahn sign style (blue for Autobahn, yellow for Bundesstraße)
Specific German road sign fonts and colors
Very high quality road surfaces especially on major routes
German speed limit sign style (white circle with red border)
tier2_identifiers: German utility infrastructure — very neat and organized
Specific German rural architecture — half-timber (Fachwerk) houses

elimination_clues.vs_Austria: Very similar. Austria has A-prefix route signs, Germany B-prefix for Bundesstraße. Austrian landscape often more mountainous. AT country code vs DE.
elimination_clues.vs_Switzerland: Switzerland uses CH country code. Swiss road signs have specific Swiss design. Switzerland is much more mountainous.
elimination_clues.vs_Netherlands: Dutch is a completely different language from German on signs. Dutch landscape is extremely flat with windmills and very distinctive.

tier1_identifiers: English only on most signs
Specific US highway shield shapes (US route shield, Interstate I-xxx blue shield)
US-style stop signs (red octagon, very standard)
Yellow school bus visible in residential areas
Fire hydrants visible on sidewalks (specific US red style)
tier2_identifiers: American mailbox style at road edge
US utility pole style — wooden, with transformers
Wide road lanes with specific US road marking patterns

elimination_clues.vs_Canada: Canada has bilingual English/French in many areas (especially Quebec, New Brunswick, federal signs). US is English only. Canadian route signs have different shapes.
elimination_clues.vs_Australia: Australian road signs use different fonts and specific AU state abbreviations. Australian gum trees are very distinctive.

tier1_identifiers: Bilingual English and French on federal signs (e.g. 'STOP / ARRET')
Specific Canadian route sign shapes (different from US shields)
Canadian provincial flags and branding on some infrastructure
Quebec: French only on most signs — most reliable Quebec identifier
Red maple leaf on some official signs and infrastructure
tier2_identifiers: Canadian road surface quality — similar to US but with provincial variation
Specific Canadian utility infrastructure

elimination_clues.vs_United_States: Bilingual STOP/ARRET signs = Canada confirmed. Quebec French-only signs = Canada confirmed. Canadian route sign shapes are different from US highway shields.

tier1_identifiers: Spanish language on signs
Specific Argentine road sign style — blue and white national colors
RN (Ruta Nacional) and RP (Ruta Provincial) prefixes on route signs
Specific Argentine utility pole style
Pampas — flat agricultural grassland horizon to horizon
tier2_identifiers: Argentine commercial truck style
Specific Argentine rural architecture

elimination_clues.vs_Chile: Chile is much more mountainous (Andes dominate). Argentine pampas are flat. Chilean RUT road signs vs Argentine RN/RP.
elimination_clues.vs_Uruguay: Almost identical. Uruguay is smaller, infrastructure slightly less developed. Hard to distinguish without city names.
elimination_clues.vs_Brazil: Brazilian signs are in Portuguese, not Spanish. Very different.

tier1_identifiers: Spanish language on signs
Dramatic Andes mountains visible to east — almost always present
Specific Chilean road sign style (similar to Argentine but Chilean)
Ruta 5 (Pan-American Highway) very long, straight, with distinctive signage
Pacific Ocean visible to west in coastal areas
Atacama Desert in north — absolutely unique barren landscape
tier2_identifiers: Specific Chilean utility pole style
Chilean commercial truck and bus design

elimination_clues.vs_Argentina: Chile much more mountainous — Andes very prominent. Argentine pampas are flat. Chile is a very narrow country so mountains or coast usually visible.
elimination_clues.vs_Peru: Very similar in some areas. Peruvian road signs use slightly different design standards. Peru has more indigenous cultural elements visible.

tier1_identifiers: Spanish language on signs
Specific Mexican road sign style — green for federal highways
MEX-prefix on federal route signs
Speed bump warning signs — very common in Mexico (topes)
Specific Mexican utility pole style — often with distinctive transformer
PEMEX gas stations — very distinctive red, green, white branding
tier2_identifiers: Mexican commercial truck and bus style
Specific Mexican rural architecture — concrete block construction

elimination_clues.vs_Guatemala: Guatemala has more mountainous terrain and different road sign standards. Mexican infrastructure generally more developed.
elimination_clues.vs_Colombia: Colombia has very different mountain terrain. Colombian cities like Medellin have distinctive infrastructure.
